newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke under fire again for plain speaking.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke under fire again for plain speaking.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke was back in the firing line on Monday after vowing not to cut taxes simply to win votes and admitting the Conservative Party had failed to deliver on key 1992 election promises.

Clarke, who was attacked by so-called Eurosceptics in his own party last week over remarks sympathetic to the European single currency, said voters would be "deeply suspicious" of any tax cuts in the November budget.
The November budget will be the last before an election which must be called by May. The Conservatives are trailing Labour by some 20 points in opinion polls.

"The public will be deeply suspicious of any tax cuts because they remember we promised tax cuts last time and unfortunately weren't able to deliver them," Clarke said in a weekend television interview.
Clarke's frank remarks handed Labour a huge boost for Monday's opening day of their annual party conference and reopened speculation about his future in the government.
"Even the chancellor admits the government can't be trusted," said Labour finance spokesman Gordon Brown.
Clarke repeated his comments on Monday, saying he hoped voters would appreciate a politician being straightforward.

"I think many of them will throw their hats in the air to hear a politician making the first priority a sensible economy and being straightforward with them about how you can get tax cuts when you can afford it," he told BBC radio.

Last week Clarke infuriated many Conservatives by saying it would be "pathetic" for Britain to delay joining a single European currency. The government's official policy is to wait and see if the single currency is to Britain's advantage before deciding whether to join.
Conservatives MPs banking on tax cuts as a last-ditch hope of winning the elections were angered by Clarke's remarks.
"I believe we should be looking in the budget for further reductions in taxes paid for by cuts in spending to re-establish our reputation as the low tax party," said Conservative John Townend.
Britain's tabloid Sun newspaper demanded to know which party Clarke was backing.
"What game is Kenneth Clarke playing? The chancellor has forgotten he's a Tory (Conservative)....Perhaps Clarke really wants Labour to win," The Sun said in an editorial.
